record.paper_title: Problems and Conjectures Presented at the Third International Conference on Permutation Patterns (University of Florida, March 7-11, 2005)
record.original_question: Let pi be a permutation of length k, and let sigma_1, sigma_2, ..., sigma_k be permutations; write pi[sigma_1, sigma_2, ..., sigma_k] for the inflation obtained by replacing the i-th entry of pi by a block order-isomorphic to sigma_i so that the blocks themselves are order-isomorphic to pi. For arbitrary permutations sigma_1, sigma_2, sigma_3 and every natural number n, is it always true that s_n(132[sigma_1, sigma_2, sigma_3]) < s_n(123[sigma_1, sigma_2, sigma_3]), that s_n(312[sigma_1, sigma_2, sigma_3]) < s_n(123[sigma_1, sigma_2, sigma_3]), and, for every t at least 2, that s_n(123[sigma_1, 12...t, sigma_3]) < s_n(123[sigma_1, t...21, sigma_3])?

evidence.quote: We define the inflation of π by σ1, σ2, . . . , σk to be the permutation obtained by replacing the ith element of π by a block order isomorphic to σi so that the blocks themselves are order isomorphic to π. We write the resulting permutation as π[σ1, σ2, . . . , σk].

Conjecture (Alex Burstein): For any permutations σ1, σ2, σ3, and any natural number n, (1) sn(132[σ1, σ2, σ3]) < sn(123[σ1, σ2, σ3]), (2) sn(312[σ1, σ2, σ3]) < sn(123[σ1, σ2, σ3]), (3) sn(123[σ1, 12 . . . t, σ3]) < sn(123[σ1, t . . . 21, σ3]) for any t ≥ 2.

artifact.status_search_result: Web searches surface other "Burstein conjectures" on pattern-avoiding permutations and inversion sequences (e.g., the 2022 resolution of Burstein's permutation conjecture on A218225), but no source was found that explicitly resolves the inequalities for inflations s_n(132[σ1,σ2,σ3]) < s_n(123[σ1,σ2,σ3]), s_n(312[σ1,σ2,σ3]) < s_n(123[σ1,σ2,σ3]), and s_n(123[σ1,12…t,σ3]) < s_n(123[σ1,t…21,σ3]). Status appears unresolved in publicly available literature.

status_evidence.snippet: Resolves a different Burstein conjecture concerning length-four pattern avoidance counted by OEIS A218225, not the inflation inequalities.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let S_n denote the set of permutations of {1,2,…,n}. A permutation σ ∈ S_n is said to contain a permutation τ ∈ S_k as a pattern if there exist indices 1 ≤ i_1 < i_2 < … < i_k ≤ n such that the values σ(i_1), σ(i_2), …, σ(i_k) appear in the same relative order as τ(1), τ(2), …, τ(k); otherwise σ avoids τ. For a permutation τ, write s_n(τ) for the number of permutations in S_n that avoid τ.

Given a permutation π of length k and permutations σ_1, σ_2, …, σ_k of arbitrary lengths m_1, m_2, …, m_k, the inflation π[σ_1, σ_2, …, σ_k] is the permutation of length m_1 + m_2 + … + m_k obtained as follows: partition the positions {1,2,…, m_1 + … + m_k} into k consecutive blocks B_1, B_2, …, B_k of sizes m_1, m_2, …, m_k respectively; fill block B_i with values forming a sub-permutation order-isomorphic to σ_i; and choose the value ranges of the blocks so that the relative order of the blocks (as wholes) is order-isomorphic to π.

For t ≥ 2 let 12…t denote the increasing permutation (1,2,…,t) and t…21 the decreasing permutation (t, t-1, …, 1).

Prove or disprove the following statements:

(1) For all permutations σ_1, σ_2, σ_3 and every positive integer n,
   s_n(132[σ_1, σ_2, σ_3]) < s_n(123[σ_1, σ_2, σ_3]).

(2) For all permutations σ_1, σ_2, σ_3 and every positive integer n,
   s_n(312[σ_1, σ_2, σ_3]) < s_n(123[σ_1, σ_2, σ_3]).

(3) For all permutations σ_1, σ_3, every integer t ≥ 2, and every positive integer n,
   s_n(123[σ_1, 12…t, σ_3]) < s_n(123[σ_1, t…21, σ_3]).
